curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: `d c y`; `dd cc yy`; `D C Y`; `p P`; counts before operators or motions; linewise vs characterwise ranges; `> < =`; `gq gw`; `.`
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Compose operators with motions, predict the affected range, put text, and make a change deliberately repeatable
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Delete two words; change to line end; duplicate a line; indent a block by motion; reflow a paragraph; repeat a prepared change
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core. Host formatting may affect `=` and `gq`, so exercises use deterministic app behavior

lessons.title: Give an operator a range
lessons.objective: Compose delete, change, and yank with learned motions and predict their characterwise ranges.

activities.title: Combine an action with a target
activities.body: Keys such as `d`, `c`, and `y` choose the action: delete, change, or copy. A following motion chooses the text that action affects.
activities.grammar: operator + motion → action over a range
activities.contrast: A motion alone travels. An operator plus that motion transforms or captures the same range.

activities.title: Delete one word range
activities.instruction: Use delete with `w` to remove the stale field.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete through the next word boundary.

hints: Delete needs a range.
Use `dw`.

feedback.success: The stale field is gone.
feedback.why: `w` supplied the characterwise range consumed by `d`.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A three-field log makes the removed word range obvious.

activities.title: Change the status in place
activities.instruction: Replace the “draft” status with “ready”.
hints: Use change rather than delete followed by insert.
Use `cwready Escape`.

feedback.success: Status updated.
feedback.why: `cw` removed the word and entered Insert mode at the same boundary.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A status row provides a natural one-word replacement.

activities.title: Capture without changing text
activities.instruction: Capture the word “ready” without changing the line.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank the word range without editing it.

hints: First move to the second field.
Use `wyw`.

feedback.success: The field is captured.
feedback.why: `y` used the same motion grammar while leaving the buffer untouched.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the unnamed register is introduced only as the destination.

provenance.languageRationale: Two log fields isolate movement followed by yank.

activities.title: Choose the larger word boundary
activities.instruction: Remove the path-like field “api/v1 ”, leaving “stale result”.
hints: The slash should remain inside one range.
Use uppercase `W` with delete.

feedback.success: The full path field is gone.
feedback.why: `W` treated punctuation as part of the whitespace-delimited range.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A path token makes the WORD boundary meaningful.

lessons.title: Operate on lines or line tails
lessons.objective: Distinguish doubled line operators from D, C, and Y shorthands.

activities.title: Repeat an operator to target a whole line
activities.body: Use `dd`, `cc`, or `yy` to delete, change, or copy a whole line. `D` and `C` act from the cursor to the line end, while `Y` copies the whole line.
activities.grammar: dd / cc / yy → whole line · D / C → tail · Y → whole line
activities.contrast: `Y` follows `yy`, not the tail-shaped behavior of `D` and `C`.

activities.title: Delete, recover, then change a tail
activities.instruction: Observe `D`, undo it, then use `C` to replace the same tail.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete from the cursor through line end.
Enter Insert mode at the end of the line.

hints: The two uppercase commands use the same tail range.

feedback.success: The tail is replaced.
feedback.why: `D` deleted the tail; `C` deleted it and entered Insert mode.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A declaration value creates a clear cursor-to-end tail.

activities.title: Replace one complete row
activities.instruction: Replace the first row with “enabled: true”.
hints: Double the change operator for a linewise range.
Use `ccenabled: true Escape`.

feedback.success: The row is replaced.
feedback.why: `cc` preserved the row boundary while replacing all of its text.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A short YAML setting is natural whole-line content.

activities.title: Duplicate a declaration
activities.instruction: Duplicate the first declaration directly below itself.

commandGroups.explanation: Put the line before the cursor line.

hints: Unlike D and C, Y is linewise.
Use `YjP`.

feedback.success: The declaration is duplicated.
feedback.why: `Y` captured a linewise register, so `P` inserted a complete row.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Adjacent declarations make linewise duplication visible.

activities.title: Remove only the middle row
activities.instruction: Remove the middle row and leave the others untouched.
hints: Use the linewise form of delete.

feedback.success: Only the unwanted row is gone.
feedback.why: Doubling `d` selected a linewise range including its newline.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Three neutral rows make the deleted line boundary unambiguous.

activities.title: Replace from cursor to line end
activities.instruction: Replace the “draft” tail with “ready”.
hints: Use the uppercase change shorthand.

feedback.success: The tail now reads ready.
feedback.why: `C` is the compact form of change to line end.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A simple assignment makes the tail boundary exact.

lessons.title: Put by register shape
lessons.objective: Use p and P with characterwise and linewise unnamed-register content.

activities.title: Put copied text before or after the cursor
activities.body: Press `p` to put text after the cursor or below the current line. Press `P` to put it before the cursor or above the current line.
activities.grammar: characterwise: P ← cursor → p · linewise: P ↑ row ↓ p
activities.contrast: The same put key uses the register's shape to choose a character or line boundary.

activities.title: Duplicate a characterwise word
activities.instruction: Yank `api` through its word end, move there, then put it after the cursor.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank through the current word end.
Put the captured characters after the cursor.

hints: A characterwise register puts next to the cursor.

feedback.success: The tag is duplicated.
feedback.why: `p` inserted the yanked characters after the word end.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; only the unnamed register is used.

provenance.languageRationale: A short tag value shows characterwise adjacency clearly.

activities.title: Duplicate a line below
activities.instruction: Leave a second copy of the append call directly below the first.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank the current line as a linewise range.
Put the linewise register below the current line.

hints: Use the doubled yank form, then lowercase put.

feedback.success: The call now appears twice, ready for the copy to be edited.
feedback.why: A linewise register is put on its own row rather than inside the current one.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fixture is unindented because automatic indentation is host-configurable.

provenance.languageRationale: Duplicating a call is the everyday reason to yank and put a whole line of code.

activities.title: Duplicate a line above
activities.instruction: Leave a second copy of the deploy call directly above the first.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank the current line as a linewise range.
Put the linewise register above the current line.

hints: Uppercase put chooses the boundary before or above.

feedback.success: The deploy call is duplicated above its original.
feedback.why: Uppercase `P` chose the row above while keeping the same linewise shape.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fixture is unindented because automatic indentation is host-configurable.

provenance.languageRationale: Two build steps make the direction of the put unambiguous.

activities.title: Move a row through the unnamed register
activities.instruction: Swap the first two statements so the connection is opened before it is validated.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete the current line into the unnamed register.
Put it back below the line the cursor landed on.

hints: Delete also updates the unnamed register.
Use `ddp`.

feedback.success: The two statements traded places.
feedback.why: A delete fills the same register a yank does, so `dd` followed by `p` is a move.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fixture is unindented because automatic indentation is host-configurable.

provenance.languageRationale: Reordering two statements is the plainest real use of delete-then-put.

lessons.title: Count actions and ranges
lessons.objective: Place counts before operators or motions and understand count multiplication.

activities.title: Use counts with operators
activities.body: Both `2dw` and `d2w` delete across two word motions. If you add a count before both the operator and motion, Vim multiplies them, so `2d3w` covers six motions.
activities.contrast: Prefer one clear count in ordinary work; multiplication explains the grammar rather than rewarding obscurity.

activities.title: Count before the operator
activities.instruction: Use `2dw` to delete the first two word ranges.
hints: Put the count before the operator.

feedback.success: Two word ranges are deleted.
feedback.why: The leading count repeated the complete `dw` action.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Number words make the counted range easy to audit.

activities.title: Count the motion instead
activities.instruction: Remove the first two words, leaving “three four”.
hints: Start the operator, then count its motion.

feedback.success: The same two ranges are gone.
feedback.why: The motion count enlarged the range supplied to one delete operator.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: The repeated fixture makes 2dw and d2w directly comparable.

activities.title: Read multiplied counts
activities.instruction: Remove the first six words, leaving only “seven”.

lines: one two three four five six seven

commandGroups.explanation: Multiply two delete repetitions by a three-word motion.

hints: The two counts multiply rather than add.
Use `2d3w`.

feedback.success: Six ranges collapse to one survivor.
feedback.why: The operator count and motion count multiplied to six word motions.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior, though a single count is usually clearer.

provenance.languageRationale: Seven number words expose the exact multiplied range.

activities.title: Replace two words as one change
activities.instruction: Replace “alpha beta” with “ready”.
hints: Count the word motion after change.
Use `c2wready Escape`.

feedback.success: Two words became one deliberate change.
feedback.why: The counted motion determined the full range before Insert mode began.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Three plain words make the replaced two-word span exact.

lessons.title: Shift a motion range
lessons.objective: Indent or unindent motion and line ranges with greater-than and less-than operators.

activities.title: Indent text left or right
activities.body: Use `>` with a motion to indent right and `<` with a motion to indent left. Repeat the operator, as in `>>`, to affect the current line.
activities.contrast: The count on `2>>` selects two lines; it does not shift one line twice.

activities.title: Shift two lines by motion
activities.instruction: Use `>j` to indent the first two rows by one two-space level.

commandGroups.explanation: Shift the range from this line through the next line.

hints: Indent is an operator; `j` supplies its range.

feedback.success: Two rows move right together.
feedback.why: The app's fixed indentation unit makes one shift exactly two spaces.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior with an app-defined two-space shift width.

provenance.languageRationale: Python-like rows make leading indentation structurally meaningful.

activities.title: Shift only this line
activities.instruction: Indent “alpha” by one level and leave “beta” alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Shift the complete current line right.

hints: Double the shift operator for the current line.

feedback.success: Only alpha moved.
feedback.why: Repeating `>` selected a linewise current-line range.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior with a two-space shift width.

provenance.languageRationale: Two bare rows expose the single shifted line.

activities.title: Pull two rows back left
activities.instruction: Remove one indentation level from “alpha” and “beta”.

commandGroups.explanation: Shift this line and the next line left.

hints: Use the left-shift operator with a downward motion.

feedback.success: The rows return to column zero.
feedback.why: `<` applied one deterministic indentation step across the `j` range.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior with a two-space shift width.

provenance.languageRationale: Leading spaces provide a measurable left shift.

activities.title: Indent exactly two rows
activities.instruction: Indent “alpha” and “beta” by one level, leaving “gamma” alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Shift two complete lines right once.

hints: The count chooses how many lines the doubled operator receives.

feedback.success: Exactly two rows are indented.
feedback.why: `2>>` selected two lines and shifted that linewise range once.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior with a two-space shift width.

provenance.languageRationale: Three rows make the two-line count visible.

lessons.title: Reindent from syntax
lessons.objective: Use equals with line and motion ranges under deterministic JavaScript indentation.

activities.title: Recalculate indentation
activities.body: The `=` operator fixes indentation for the target range. These lessons use two-space indentation so the result is predictable.
activities.contrast: `>` adds one level blindly; `=` recalculates the appropriate level from syntax.

activities.title: Repair a block entry
activities.instruction: Use `=j` to reindent the block opener and its first statement.

commandGroups.explanation: Reindent through the next logical line.

hints: Give the reindent operator a downward range.

feedback.success: The statement aligns with its block.
feedback.why: Syntax-aware `=` computed the statement's two-space indentation.

activities.portability: The app pins JavaScript parsing and a two-space indentation unit for deterministic behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript block is supported by the bundled syntax parser.

activities.title: Normalize one statement
activities.instruction: Correct the indentation of “run();” without changing the surrounding lines.
hints: Double the operator for one whole line.

feedback.success: The call has the correct block indent.
feedback.why: `==` recalculated the current line rather than shifting it by a relative amount.

activities.portability: Deterministic for the bundled JavaScript parser.

provenance.languageRationale: An over-indented JavaScript call proves recalculation rather than blind shifting.

activities.title: Normalize two statements
activities.instruction: Correct the indentation of both statements inside the block.
hints: Count the motion supplied to equals.

feedback.success: Both calls align inside the block.
feedback.why: The counted motion expanded the reindent range to three logical lines.

activities.portability: Deterministic for the bundled JavaScript parser.

provenance.languageRationale: Two adjacent calls make the counted range clear.

activities.title: Reindent the complete nested buffer
activities.instruction: Correct the indentation throughout the nested block.
hints: Anchor the operator at the first line, then give it the last-line motion.
Use `gg=G`.

feedback.success: The nested structure is aligned.
feedback.why: Buffer motions supplied one complete deterministic range to equals.

activities.portability: Deterministic for the bundled JavaScript parser.

provenance.languageRationale: Nested JavaScript braces provide an unambiguous indentation hierarchy.

lessons.title: Reflow text deliberately
lessons.objective: Format motion ranges with gq or gw and distinguish their final cursor positions.
lessons.trackNote: Optional — depends on configuration or file type: `gq` and `gw` wrap to the buffer's `textwidth`, so with the default of zero they reflow to the window width instead of a stable column; these activities set an explicit width of forty so the result is deterministic.

activities.title: Wrap text to a fixed width
activities.body: Both `gq` and `gw` wrap a target range. `gq` moves the cursor after that range, while `gw` returns the cursor to its original position.
activities.grammar: gq + motion → reflow and land after · gw + motion → reflow and keep cursor
activities.contrast: Choose by the cursor position needed for the next command, not by text output alone.

activities.title: Reflow and land after
activities.instruction: Use `gqj` to format both prose lines to forty columns.

lines: A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for practice.
A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for

commandGroups.explanation: Reflow this line and the next, then land after the result.

lines: A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for

hints: Use the reflow operator whose cursor moves after the result.

feedback.success: The prose is wrapped at a stable width.
feedback.why: `gq` formatted the `j` range and placed the cursor at the final formatted line.

activities.portability: The app fixes textwidth at forty columns for deterministic behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral prose makes hard wrapping the only transformation.

activities.title: Reflow and keep your place
activities.instruction: Reflow the prose to the practice width while keeping the cursor in place.

lines: A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for practice.
A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for

commandGroups.explanation: Reflow the two-line range but retain the original cursor.

lines: A clear formatter joins nearby words and
wraps them at a stable width for

hints: Choose the reflow operator that keeps the cursor.

feedback.success: The prose changed while the cursor stayed put.
feedback.why: `gw` shares the formatting behavior of `gq` but preserves the original position.

activities.portability: The app fixes textwidth at forty columns for deterministic behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Repeating the gq fixture isolates the cursor difference.

activities.title: Wrap one long sentence
activities.instruction: Reflow the long sentence to the practice width.

lines: This deliberately long sentence wraps into readable lines at the configured practice width.
into readable lines at the configured
into readable lines at the configured

hints: Repeat the final operator key for a current-line range.

feedback.success: One long line becomes three readable lines.
feedback.why: `gqq` is the current-line form of the reflow operator.

activities.portability: The app fixes textwidth at forty columns for deterministic behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: One prose sentence demonstrates linewise hard wrapping without syntax effects.

activities.title: Reflow a four-line range
activities.instruction: Reflow the four-line paragraph to the practice width.

lines: with a stable range and keeps
Reliable formatting starts with a stable
range and keeps the resulting prose

commandGroups.explanation: Reflow from this line through three downward motions.

lines: Reliable formatting starts with a stable
range and keeps the resulting prose

hints: The range spans the current row plus three more.
Use `gq3j`.

feedback.success: The paragraph now uses stable line lengths.
feedback.why: The counted motion supplied all four source lines to one reflow operation.

activities.portability: The app fixes textwidth at forty columns for deterministic behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Four short prose lines make joining and rewrapping visible.

lessons.title: Replay one finished change
lessons.objective: Use dot to replay a complete prepared change after simple movement.

activities.title: Repeat the last change with dot
activities.body: Press `.` to repeat the last finished edit, including text typed in Insert mode. Move to a similar target before pressing dot.
activities.contrast: This unit introduces replay. Unit 10 later teaches how to design robust repeat workflows around find, search, and Ex commands.

activities.title: Change once, replay once
activities.instruction: Rename the receiver on both calls from “draft” to “live”, repeating the change rather than retyping it.

commandGroups.explanation: Change the word under the cursor.
Complete the change so dot has something to replay.
Move to the start of the next line.

hints: Finish the first change before moving.
Use `cwnew Escape`, move to the second value, then `.`.

feedback.success: Both calls now use the new receiver.
feedback.why: Dot replayed the finished change — the operator, its range, and the typed text — at the new position.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Renaming a receiver on consecutive calls is the change most worth repeating with dot.

activities.title: Remove both debug rows
activities.instruction: Remove both logging calls and keep the run call.

commandGroups.explanation: Replay the deletion on the line that moved up.

hints: After `dd`, the next debug row becomes current.
Press dot once.

feedback.success: Only the run call remains.
feedback.why: The next line moved under the cursor, so the repeat needed no movement at all.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Removing leftover logging is the deletion a reader most expects to repeat.

activities.title: Terminate every row
activities.instruction: Give all three declarations their missing semicolons.

commandGroups.explanation: Append at the end of the line.

hints: Make the first append one complete change.
Use `A; Escape j . j .`.

feedback.success: Every declaration is terminated.
feedback.why: `A` made the insertion position part of the change, so dot found the right column on each line.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Adding missing statement terminators is the classic line-tail change to repeat.

activities.title: Update every zero
activities.instruction: Change every initial value from zero to one.

commandGroups.explanation: Replace the character under the cursor.
Move down one line, keeping the column.
Move down one line, keeping the column.

hints: `r1` is already a complete Normal-mode change.
Move down and press dot for each remaining zero.

feedback.success: All three values were corrected.
feedback.why: The aligned column meant `j` alone was enough positioning between repeats.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Three aligned assignments let one column be corrected without any movement beyond `j`.

lessons.title: Choose the range, shape, and follow-up
lessons.objective: Integrate operator choice, linewise putting, counts, formatting, and repeat.

activities.title: Choose the action, target, and next position
activities.body: First choose what to do, then select the smallest reliable target. After the edit, check where the cursor landed and what text was saved for a later put.
activities.grammar: action → range → shape → landing → optional reuse
activities.contrast: Efficiency comes from a dependable command sentence, not from the shortest mysterious key sequence.

activities.title: Copy a header before a later row
activities.instruction: Copy the check call so it also runs immediately before the second step.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank the current line as a linewise range.
Put the linewise register above the current line.

hints: Preserve line shape through yank and put.

feedback.success: The check now runs before the second step as well.
feedback.why: A counted motion carried the cursor and `P` chose the side of the destination row.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fixture is unindented because automatic indentation is host-configurable.

provenance.languageRationale: Repeating a guard call before a later step is a real reason to yank one line and put it elsewhere.

activities.title: Indent two adjacent pairs
activities.instruction: Indent all four rows by one level, working in adjacent pairs.

commandGroups.explanation: Reach the start of the second pair.

hints: Prepare one `>j` range, then move to the next pair.
Use `>j2j.`.

feedback.success: Both pairs share one indentation change.
feedback.why: Dot replayed the complete shift operator and its motion range.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior with a two-space shift width.

provenance.languageRationale: Four Python-like rows form two visible indentation ranges.

activities.title: Change three aligned fields
activities.instruction: Rename the variable on all three lines from “old” to “new”.

commandGroups.explanation: Change the word under the cursor.
Move to the start of the next line.
Move to the start of the next line.

hints: Make the first change complete before moving.
Use the line start as a stable landing for each dot.

feedback.success: Every assignment uses the new name.
feedback.why: One finished change plus deliberate repositioning covered the whole block.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Renaming one variable down a short block is the change worth repeating rather than retyping.

activities.title: Move two rows to the end
activities.instruction: Move both logging calls below the work they describe.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete two lines into the unnamed register.
Move to the row the block should follow.
Put the two-line register below it.

hints: Count the doubled delete so the register remains linewise.
Use `2ddjp`.

feedback.success: Both logging calls now follow the work.
feedback.why: The count made the delete a two-line linewise range, and the put restored it in one piece.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fixture is unindented because automatic indentation is host-configurable.

provenance.languageRationale: Moving a pair of logging calls after the work they describe exercises a counted delete and a put together.

activities.title: Choose the dependable command
activities.prompt: You must duplicate the current complete line below itself. Which command preserves the correct range shape?
activities.explanation: `yy` creates linewise register content, so `p` inserts a complete row below rather than inline.

activities.title: Actions become dependable sentences
activities.body: You can now choose an operator, describe its range, predict characterwise or linewise register shape, format deterministic text, and replay one complete change.
takeaways: Compose d, c, y, shifts, reindent, and reflow with explicit ranges.
Let linewise versus characterwise shape predict p and P behavior.
Use counts clearly and remember that two count positions multiply.
Prepare and finish one change before introducing dot-repeat.

reference.purpose: Delete, change, or yank a characterwise motion range.

reference.purpose: Operate on complete lines or cursor-to-end tails.

reference.purpose: Hard-wrap text to the configured text width.
